demos.name: 3.0 Getting around the Playground
demos.description: The workbook used in the walkthrough at the start of Chapter 3: a state ψ, a box f and an effect π in the Diagram Editor (with its ∘⊗ reading switched on), the same diagram in Dirac notation, and a first proof — moving a box changes nothing, because only connectivity matters (PQP Cor. 3.5).

demos.name: 3.1 Composing processes
demos.description: Parallel (⊗) and sequential (∘) composition (PQP §3.2). The interchange law (g₁ ⊗ g₂) ∘ (f₁ ⊗ f₂) = (g₁ ∘ f₁) ⊗ (g₂ ∘ f₂), equation (3.16), is one picture drawn twice; an effect followed by a state is the two side by side; and a circuit — H, then CNOT — shown with its ∘⊗ layers.

demos.name: 3.2 States, effects and numbers
demos.description: PQP §3.4: a state meets an effect and a number pops out. Here ⟨+|0⟩ = 1/√2 in the Diagram Editor, its Dirac form and its Numbers; ⟨1|0⟩ is the impossible number 0; and 2·f ≈ f, equal up to a number (PQP Def. 3.39).

demos.name: 3.1 A state, a box and an effect
demos.description: Blank starter: build ψ → f → π and read it in Dirac notation.

demos.name: 3.2 Side by side, one after the other
demos.description: Two empty diagrams: build f ⊗ g and g ∘ f and compare their ∘⊗ readings and Dirac forms.

demos.name: 3.3 Numbers from states and effects
demos.description: Blank starter: plug basis states into basis effects and read off the numbers.

demos.name: 3.4 Only connectivity matters
demos.description: Four diagrams and two proofs to finish: which pairs are equal, and why?

demos.name: 3.5 Equal up to a number
demos.description: A proof that fails with = : make it hold, then see why zero is special.

demos.name: 3.6 A circuit is a diagram
demos.description: A two-gate circuit: find its layers and write it as one ∘/⊗ formula.

demos.name: 3.7 Diagram substitution
demos.description: A goal proof: replace part of a diagram using an equation (PQP §3.1.5).

demos.name: 3.8 Dirac notation on one line
demos.description: Three diagrams to write in Dirac notation and verify.

demos.name: 3.9 Zero eats everything
demos.description: A goal proof about the zero number (PQP §3.4.2), plus a question on paper.

demos.name: 3.10 What the checker checks
demos.description: Two look-alike claims, one ✓ and one ✗: diagram equations vs process equations.

demos.name: Getting started: the Bell state
demos.description: One state, four ways. The circuit (H, then CNOT, on |00⟩) prepares the Bell state; the Diagram Editor shows the same circuit as a PQP diagram; the proof simplifies that diagram, one checked rewrite at a time, to a cup; and the Dirac editor writes it out — click a saved formula to check another way of writing the same state. Edit the circuit and its diagram and Dirac follow (the proof keeps its own copies).

demos.name: Spider rules
demos.description: The basic ZX rewrites as checked proofs: spider fusion, colour change, π-copy, and identity removal. Each uses symbolic phases, checked for random values.

demos.name: Snake equations
demos.description: A cup followed by a cap straightens to a plain wire — the snake (yanking) equation — and a box f slides through the bend. f is symbolic: the check holds for random choices of f.

demos.name: Sliding round bends
demos.description: Proposition 4.30 of Picturing Quantum Processes: a box slides round a cup or a cap and comes out as its transpose (drawn rotated 180°). Each step here was made with the slide handle (select a box on a cup or cap leg and press S), and every step is checked for a random box. The necklace strings three boxes along a snake, slides them onto one strand, and yanks it straight.

demos.name: Pulling wires taut
demos.description: In Picturing Quantum Processes wires are pieces of string: only what connects to what matters. Pull a diagram taut and every snake straightens, needless crossings undo, and each box riding a wire slides along it — coming out transposed if it went round a bend. Every proof step here was made by “⟿ Taut step” and is checked equal to the one before. On the right is a tangle to try yourself: press T (or ⟿) to watch it pull taut, scrub back and forth, then Apply.

demos.name: Measurement and discarding
demos.description: The doubled picture of Picturing Quantum Processes: thick wires are quantum, thin wires classical. White dots with thin and thick legs measure (thick in, thin out), encode (thin in, thick out), copy and delete; ⏚ discards. The proofs: measuring then deleting is discarding, encoding then discarding is deleting, measuring then encoding is decoherence, discarding a pure state gives the Born rule, and a doubled unitary is causal.

demos.name: Causality
demos.description: Proofs that need assumptions and sums (PQP ch. 8). A proof can assume things about its symbols — Φ causal, U unitary — shown in the bar above the steps; every check then uses random values satisfying them. Composing causal processes is causal; measuring is causal (a sum over a basis, Σᵢ); a unitary undoes itself; a doubled isometry is causal; and Σᵢ |i⟩⟨i| is the identity.

demos.name: GHZ state
demos.description: Three qubits: H, then a staircase of CNOTs, prepares (|000⟩ + |111⟩)/√2. Compare the circuit with its PQP diagram — each CNOT is a green and a red spider joined by a leg.

demos.name: Quantum teleportation
demos.description: Alice holds a qubit (q0) and half of a Bell pair (q1); Bob holds the other half (q2). She measures q0 and q1 in the Bell basis — the wires turn classical (double lines) — and Bob corrects with an X and a Z controlled by her two bits. Because the circuit measures, its PQP diagram is doubled: thick quantum wires, thin classical ones, white dots for the measurements and the classical controls. The proof checks that the whole process, with the bits discarded, is just a wire: the state arrives intact.
